newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire protesters defy armoured cars in capital.
newsitem.headline: Zaire protesters defy armoured cars in capital.

text.p: Supporters of Zaire Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi broke through cordons of troops who used armoured cars on Monday to halt a march on parliament which is trying to oust the controversial politician, witnesses said.
Several thousand protesters set up barricades of burning tyres in the streets of the capital's teeming shantytowns.
Para-military gendarmes used armoured vehicles and teargas to disperse more than a thousand protesters in one of several groups trying to stop Monday's opening session of parliament.
"There were about 1,000 demonstrators heading towards parliament. Police fired teargas but they kept going and were joined by more people," one witness said.
Smaller groups of pro-Tshisekedi militants advanced on the main parliament building from different directions, before being pushed back and returning again.
Armoured vehicles circulated around the building, homing in on small crowds and driving them back.
They were joined by pickup trucks full of protesters carrying palm leaves and chanting support for Tshisekedi.
Nearby close to the national radio station and information ministry protesters blocked traffic with flaming tyres on the main 24th of November Avenue.
"Tshisekedi or nothing. Tshisekedi or total revolution," a civil servant amongst the protesters shouted.
Some gendarmes deployed to disperse the crowds were visibly dragging their feet after being emptied out of trucks onto the streets where the air was full of teargas.
"We too support the prime minister. We do not want him to be toppled," one gendarme said.
Soldiers prevented lawmakers from entering parliament earlier on, national radio reported. It was not clear if they did this in support of the prime minister.

Tshisekedi, a radical politician and President Mobutu Sese Seko's chief political rival, was appointed last week but parliament has initiated moves to remove him because of his unilateral decision to dissolve the assembly.
The opposition bloc that returned Tshisekedi to the job he had been sacked from four years ago joined rivals on Saturday to try to oust the prime minister.
Parliament planned to use the opening session to start procedures that could lead to the prime minister's removal.
Tshisekedi has particularly angered Mobutu's supporters, who dominate parliament, by completely excluding them from a cabinet he announced on Thursday, his first day in office.
The political turmoil sparked by Tshisekedi's actions has complicated Zaire's crisis as rebels advancing in the east and south look set to capture the country's second city Lubumbashi.

Rebels now hold more than a third of the vast nation since taking up arms last October. There is no sign of a breakthrough in the first direct talks between the warring parties, which began in South Africa on Saturday.
